frontmatter.title: Symbolic FEM and Adjoint Forms
frontmatter.description: Every implicit solve in Underworld3 is a residual written in SymPy, and its Newton solver assembles the tangent stiffness from four symbolic derivative blocks. We show that the same blocks give the adjoint: one transposed linear solve, and an integral for each parameter, yield the derivative of a misfit with respect to every parameter of the model at once.

children.value: In this article, we will see how the underworld3 sympy formulation combined with the PETSc finite element, strong-form framework builds model derivatives which can solve non-linear problems using a Newton method. This requires us to calculate the local derivative of the model with respect to the unknowns so that we know the direction to move towards a better solution.

If we differentiate the prediction a model makes with respect to one of its parameters, then we can determine how sensitive the prediction is to changes in that parameter and therefore whether the model can be used to constrain the value of that parameter. Similarly, model derivatives are used in data assimilation to determine how to adjust a model’s parameters so it better fits the observations we have

That the two agree is Maxwell–Betti reciprocity: the
work done by one force through the displacements of another equals the work
done by the second through the displacements of the first. The transpose is
what makes it true for a problem whose stiffness is not symmetric.

So the adjoint is cheap in parameters and dear in misfits. One solve for ten
parameters or a thousand; another solve for every additional misfit. That
suits a model with many dials and one thing you care about, which is the usual
shape of the problem.

The Newton update, the forward sensitivity and the adjoint are three linear
solves with the same matrix and different right-hand sides:

K\,\delta u = -R, \qquad\quad
K\,\frac{\mathrm d u}{\mathrm d m} = -\frac{\partial R}{\partial m},
\qquad\quad
K^{T}\mu = -\Big(\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}\Big)^{T} .
